title: Esther 7:1–6
context: Esther 7:1–6 records Esther’s second banquet. The king again asks her petition, promising up to half the kingdom. Esther asks for her life and the life of her people, because they have been sold to be destroyed, killed, and wiped out. She says she would have kept silent if they had only been sold as slaves. The king demands to know who has dared to do this, and Esther names the adversary and enemy, the wicked Haman, who is terrified before the king and queen. Esther’s courage fulfills the risk she accepted in 4:14–16. God is not named, and the narrator does not describe Esther praying here, though she had called for a fast in 4:16. Both traditions read Esther’s intercession for her people as courageous faithfulness, and they see the passage as shared ground.

verses.text: So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen.
verses.arminianNotes: The king and Haman come to Esther’s banquet. Arminian readers see Esther following through with her plan, showing patience and courage as she prepares to make her request.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the banquet as the setting for the decisive turn in the story. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground, noting the tension created by the events of chapter 6.

verses.text: The king said again to Esther on the second day at the banquet of wine, “What is your petition, queen Esther? It shall be granted you. What is your request? Even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.”
verses.arminianNotes: On the second day the king again asks Esther her petition, promising up to half the kingdom. Arminians see the king’s favor toward Esther opening the way for her to plead for her people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the king’s repeated offer as part of the way events unfold in Esther’s favor. Both traditions read the promise of half the kingdom as a customary expression of generosity rather than a literal offer.

verses.text: Then Esther the queen answered, “If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it pleases the king, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther asks that her life and the life of her people be given to her. Arminian readers see her courage in identifying with her people and risking her own position, as she had resolved to do in 4:16.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Esther as an example of faithful intercession. Both traditions recall Mordecai’s words in 4:14 about her coming to the kingdom at such a time, and they read her request as shared ground.

verses.text: For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for male and female slaves, I would have held my peace, although the adversary could not have compensated for the king’s loss.”
verses.arminianNotes: Esther says she and her people have been sold to be destroyed, killed, and wiped out, and she would have kept silent if they had only been sold as slaves. Arminians see her carefully framing the request to show the seriousness of the threat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The last part of the verse is difficult in Hebrew, and translations render it differently, so both traditions avoid building on its exact sense and read the verse as Esther’s plea for her people’s lives.

verses.text: Then King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen, “Who is he, and where is he who dared presume in his heart to do so?”
verses.arminianNotes: The king demands to know who has dared to do this. Arminian readers see the king’s outrage at a plot against his queen, though he had approved the decree without knowing its full meaning (3:8–11).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the irony that the king had authorized the plan himself. Both traditions read the verse as building to the moment when Esther names the enemy.

verses.text: Esther said, “An adversary and an enemy, even this wicked Haman!” Then Haman was afraid before the king and the queen.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther names the adversary and enemy, the wicked Haman, who is terrified before the king and queen. Arminians see courage in confronting evil openly, and they see the moment of exposure Haman had not foreseen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversal of power as Haman becomes afraid. Both traditions read the verse as the climax of Esther’s courage and as shared ground about evil being brought to light.
